subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Positive Reciprocity
description: A short lesson to help you apply Positive Reciprocity.

hook.text: Waiters who left a mint with the bill got 3% higher tips. Two mints got 14%. A personalized mint got 23%.

buildup.text: Positive reciprocity: when someone gives us something, we feel compelled to give back. The urge is automatic.

discovery.text: Regan's study showed that people who received a small unsolicited favor bought twice as many raffle tickets.

twist.text: The gift doesn't need to match. A small favor can trigger a disproportionately large return.

climax.text: Free samples, gifts, and favors exploit this. Be aware when generosity precedes a sales pitch. The debt is the product.

punchline.text: The free gift is never free. It buys your reciprocity.

quiz.question: What happens when a small unsolicited favor is given?
options: People feel no obligation to reciprocate
People often return a disproportionately large favor
People always return the exact same value

details.summary: Positive reciprocity is the human tendency to return favors and reward kindness. When someone does something nice for us, we feel obligated to reciprocate, creating cycles of mutual generosity that sustain cooperation and economic exchange beyond pure self-interest.
details.whyItMatters: Positive reciprocity is the foundation of trust-based commerce. It explains why free samples generate sales, why gifts create obligations, and why workplace generosity produces loyalty that exceeds what monetary incentives alone can achieve.
takeaways: Kindness generates a felt obligation to reciprocate in kind
Reciprocity sustains long-term economic relationships beyond contracts
Free gifts and samples exploit reciprocity norms to drive purchases

faq.question: How do businesses exploit positive reciprocity?
faq.answer: Free samples, complimentary upgrades, and unexpected bonuses create a felt obligation to reciprocate. A waiter who brings a free mint with the check receives a larger tip. The gift feels personal, triggering the reciprocity norm even in commercial settings.

faq.question: Is positive reciprocity culturally universal?
faq.answer: Yes, though its forms vary. Gift exchange is documented in every human society. The specific rules about timing, proportionality, and context differ across cultures, but the fundamental norm of returning favors appears to be a human universal.
